blocks.text: 执行摘要

inlines.text: Wiz Research、Ikotas Labs、Metnir、Rapid7 和 Xint 各自独立发现了 NGINX 中的两个严重远程代码执行漏洞。NGINX 是一款用于接收流量并将其路由到生产应用和 API 的软件。
在现代 Web 架构中，NGINX 常被默认用作前门，负责处理 HTTPS 并将传入流量路由到正确的应用或 API。作为
全球使用最广泛的开源 Web 服务器
攻击者一旦利用成功，就能控制受影响的 NGINX 服务器、窃取敏感数据、篡改网站或中断服务。
这两个漏洞编号为 CVE-2026-123633 和 CVE-2026-123007，均被评为严重级别，CVSS 4.0 评分为 9.2。漏洞存在于 NGINX 本身。即使网站和 API 自身的应用代码是安全的，也可能受到影响。
两个漏洞都要求受影响的 NGINX 服务器启用 HTTP/2。
其他条件见下文。CVE-2026-123007 影响的最早版本可追溯到 2015 年的 NGINX 1.9.5。
我们已将发现报告给 NGINX 背后的公司 F5，并与该公司安全团队合作进行修复和协同披露。各组织应识别受影响的部署，并在安全更新发布后及时应用。
我们建议将受影响的 NGINX 部署更新到包含多项安全修复的最新版本。

blocks.text: 整数下溢漏洞可追溯到 2015 年的 NGINX 1.9.5，也就是说它在代码里藏了十多年。释放后使用漏洞则存在了近六年。与我们上个月报告的 PHP2Shell 漏洞以及昨天由 Calif 披露的 Java4Shell 一样，这些都是内存安全缺陷，历来极难发现和利用。要找到它们，往往需要追踪内存操作与多条代码路径之间微妙的交互。多年来，这种复杂性本身就构成了一道实际屏障。而 AI 正在从根本上瓦解这道屏障。随着 AI 模型越来越擅长追踪这些交互，研究人员和攻击者都能发现支撑互联网和现代应用的软件中长期存在的缺陷。多个独立研究团队在 PHP 和 NGINX 中发现了同样的漏洞，而这些漏洞已在代码中存在多年，这让上述转变尤为引人注目。随着 AI 能力提升，每一代新模型都可能挖出更复杂的漏洞，而这些漏洞此前在实际中根本无法触及。复杂性不再能作为阻止发现或利用的屏障。这不仅改变了哪些漏洞能被发现，也改变了长期存在的风险能以多快的速度变成真实威胁。

blocks.text: NGINX 是什么？
NGINX 是全球使用最广泛的开源 Web 服务器，为超过 2.25 亿个网站提供支持。它通常作为网站和 API 前方的反向代理使用。在这一角色中，NGINX 接收传入请求，根据配置将其转发到相应的应用服务器，再把响应返回给用户。

blocks.text: NGINX 也能直接提供 Web 内容，并充当负载均衡器，把流量分发到多台服务器。单个 NGINX 部署可以服务多个应用，从而成为其背后网站和 API 的共享入口。

blocks.text: 漏洞详情
这两个漏洞都是 NGINX 处理 HTTP/2 流量时出现的内存安全问题。在 CVE-2026-123633 中，连接的内存已被释放，但请求仍需要使用它，从而形成释放后重用（use-after-free）。在 CVE-2026-123007 中，流量控制计数出错，导致无效的内存拷贝。两者都可能让攻击者无需认证就在 NGINX 服务器上远程执行代码。

blocks.text: 与其他内存安全问题一样，这类漏洞很难远程利用，攻击者需要泄露内存地址、正确地整理和塑造堆布局，还要应对不同的 NGINX 版本、构建和配置。现实中，攻击者未必需要针对每一种配置，我们在 PHP2Shell 中就看到，大规模攻击最初针对的是打包产品，许多客户使用的正是完全相同的构建和配置。有动机的攻击者可能会为特定目标量身定制利用程序。

NGINX 为关键网站和应用处理流量，其核心缺陷的影响远远超出单一服务。这项研究再次表明，AI 能够发现广泛部署的基础设施中的严重漏洞。这些漏洞本就存在，是 AI 帮我们找到了它们。

blocks.text: Executive Summary

inlines.text: Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs.
NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the
world's most widely used open-source web server
Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure.
Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.
Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015.

We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released.
We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes.

blocks.text: Overview

Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services.

Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules.

blocks.text: The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell, disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.

blocks.text: Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out.

blocks.text: What is NGINX?

NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server, powering more than 225 million websites. It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user.

blocks.text: NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer, distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it.

blocks.text: The Vulnerabilities

Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

blocks.text: Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution.

blocks.text: Technical deep dive
CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

inlines.text: CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable

blocks.text: NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

inlines.text: NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts.

blocks.text: We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest:

When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing. However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close.

blocks.text: Triggering the use-after-free
Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

inlines.text: Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this.

blocks.text: Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection(). When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request.

blocks.text: Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free.

blocks.text: CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow
Returning credit for unsent data

HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window.

inlines.text: HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called

blocks.text: When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

inlines.text: When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued,
removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance:

blocks.text: h2c->send_window += window;

This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur.

blocks.text: The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update(), which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

inlines.text: , which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit:

blocks.text: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window)

The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases.

blocks.text: From an invalid length to remote code execution

inlines.text: From an invalid length to remote code execution

blocks.text: The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer.

blocks.text: When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server.

blocks.text: We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module.

blocks.text: Exploitation

To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

inlines.text: To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time.

blocks.text: Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets.

blocks.text: Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration.

blocks.text: Conclusion

With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

inlines.text: With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them.

blocks.text: As we saw with PHP2Shell, AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve.

blocks.text: The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it.
